title: Truckstop Phishing Alert: Protect Freight Platform Accounts | Hermes Insights
description: Truckstop posted a September 22 security alert warning customers about phishing emails that imitate account, security, or billing verification. Hermes turns the alert into a concise carrier and dispatcher account-safety checklist.
h1: Truckstop warned about phishing emails targeting freight-platform users. What should carriers check?
conciseAnswer: Truckstop says customers have received phishing emails asking them to click links to verify security or billing information. The company says those messages did not come from Truckstop and that legitimate Truckstop email comes from @truckstop.com or e.truckstop.com. If a user clicked one of the reported phishing links, Truckstop advises changing both the Truckstop and email-account passwords immediately.
explanation: What changed: Truckstop published a September 22, 2026 security alert after reports of phishing emails sent to its customers. The messages asked recipients to click a link to verify information for security or billing purposes. Truckstop states that these emails were phishing attempts and were not sent by Truckstop.

Why it matters: freight operations depend on trusted access to load boards, email, broker and carrier communications. A compromised platform or email account can turn an ordinary load-search workflow into an account-security and fraud problem. Historical Hermes operating material is used only for the general pattern that verification should happen before an operational action; no private account, contact, load, rate, or credential information is reused here.

What to do: check the sender domain before opening verification links, navigate to the platform directly instead of relying on an unexpected email link, and treat unusual billing or security requests as a verification event. Truckstop says its legitimate email comes from @truckstop.com or e.truckstop.com. If one of the reported phishing links was clicked, change the Truckstop and email passwords immediately and review the account for suspicious activity.

Result: the team gets a simple verification rule before acting on account-security messages. That reduces avoidable credential exposure without assuming that every unusual email is fraudulent or that a sender display name proves authenticity. Source/date: Truckstop security alert, September 22, 2026.
takeaways: Truckstop warned on September 22 about phishing emails requesting security or billing verification
Truckstop says legitimate company email comes from @truckstop.com or e.truckstop.com
If a reported phishing link was clicked, Truckstop advises changing both the Truckstop and email passwords immediately
Verify account-security requests through the platform directly before taking action

title: Meta Scam Enforcement: What Brands Should Protect | Hermes Insights
description: Meta reported new September 2026 scam-network enforcement across Facebook and Instagram, including action against shell pages and e-commerce scam infrastructure. Hermes translates the update into a practical brand-account and admin-security checklist.
h1: Meta is removing scam infrastructure at scale. What should legitimate brands protect?
conciseAnswer: Meta reported that 2026 information sharing with the Singapore Police Force led to action against more than 113,000 fraud- and scam-connected entities and pages, more than 33,600 e-commerce scam entities, and over 3.6 million shell pages before use. Meta also says it has removed 65 million scam ads so far this year, 94% before user reports. For legitimate businesses, the operational lesson is account security, controlled admin access, consistent owned identities, and rapid verification of suspicious messages or impersonation—not a promise of reach or ranking.
explanation: What changed: Meta published a new September 2026 update describing coordinated scam disruption with the Singapore Police Force. Meta says information sharing in 2026 led to action against more than 113,000 fraud- and scam-connected entities and pages, more than 33,600 e-commerce scam entities, and over 3.6 million shell pages before they could be used. Meta also reports 65 million scam ads removed so far this year, with 94% removed before anyone reported them.

Why it matters: legitimate brands compete for attention inside the same environment where impersonation, fake promotions, deceptive links, shell pages, and account compromise can erode trust. title: U.S. Diesel at $6.529/Gallon: Carrier Route Planning | Hermes
description: EIA reported U.S. on-highway diesel at $6.529 per gallon for September 21, 2026, up $0.244 in one week. Hermes connects the latest fuel move to deadhead control, lane economics, and carrier rate decisions.
h1: U.S. diesel reached $6.529 per gallon. What changes for carrier route planning?
conciseAnswer: EIA reported the U.S. average on-highway diesel price at $6.529 per gallon for September 21, 2026, up $0.244 from $6.285 one week earlier and $2.780 above the year-earlier level. That does not create one universal rate target, but it makes empty miles, reload probability, route selection, timing, and fuel assumptions more important in every load decision.
explanation: What changed: the U.S. Energy Information Administration released its September 22 update with a national on-highway diesel average of $6.529 per gallon for September 21, up from $6.285 on September 14. The one-week increase was $0.244 per gallon, and the national average was $2.780 above the year-earlier level. Regional prices also remained materially different, so one national number should be treated as a cost benchmark rather than a lane quote.

Why it matters: fuel exposure compounds weak route decisions. Historical Hermes dispatch material repeatedly treated route planning, deadhead reduction, broker negotiation, pickup and delivery verification, and the next reload as connected operating decisions. With a higher fuel benchmark, an attractive loaded rate can still produce weak economics if the truck travels too far empty, lands in a weak reload area, waits through an inefficient appointment window, or must reposition again after delivery. The archive contributes the decision pattern only; no old promised rate, commission, earnings level, customer detail, or tool claim is reused as current truth.

What to do: calculate the movement as a route, not as a headline rate. Separate loaded miles from deadhead to pickup and likely repositioning after delivery. Use a current fuel assumption appropriate to the truck and route, then account for tolls, time, equipment fit, appointment risk, payment terms, and the quality of the next move. Where regional fuel prices differ substantially, update the route assumption instead of applying the national average mechanically.

Result: the carrier or dispatcher gets a repeatable operating decision instead of a reactive fuel rule. A counteroffer can be tied to actual route economics—empty-mile exposure, timing, equipment, destination and current fuel assumptions—rather than simply citing a national diesel headline. That makes the load review more defensible without claiming every broker, lane or customer should absorb the same adjustment.

Then versus now: Hermes historical operating material already emphasized reducing deadhead and understanding where the truck can go next. The September 21, 2026 EIA data increases the cost of getting those decisions wrong, but it does not change the method: verify the lane, model the full movement, compare realistic alternatives, negotiate from the operating picture, and re-check assumptions when fuel or market conditions move.
takeaways: EIA put the U.S. on-highway diesel average at $6.529 per gallon for September 21, up $0.244 week over week
The national average was $2.780 per gallon above the year-earlier level
High diesel prices increase the importance of deadhead and reload planning; they do not create one universal carrier rate
Evaluate the full movement: loaded miles, empty miles, fuel, tolls, timing, equipment fit, payment terms and the likely next load

faq.question: Does $6.529 diesel mean every load rate should rise by the same amount?
faq.answer: No. The EIA figure is a national fuel-price benchmark, not a lane-specific rate instruction. The effect on a load depends on the truck, miles, deadhead, route, timing, equipment, tolls, reload options and other operating costs.

faq.answer: EIA reported $6.529 per gallon for September 21, 2026 versus $6.285 on September 14, an increase of $0.244 per gallon.

faq.question: Why does deadhead matter more when fuel is expensive?
faq.answer: Empty miles consume fuel and time without producing loaded revenue. When the fuel assumption rises, unnecessary positioning and weak reload planning can have a larger effect on the economics of the full trip.

title: Cloudflare Disallow AI Training: Keep Search Visibility | Hermes
description: Cloudflare introduced a Disallow AI Training control intended to keep accountable mixed-use crawlers available for search while refusing AI-training use. Hermes explains how to protect training preferences without accidentally blocking search discovery.
h1: Cloudflare can now separate search discovery from AI training. What should site owners change?
conciseAnswer: Cloudflare announced a Disallow AI Training setting on September 15, 2026. Cloudflare says the setting publishes a no-training preference through Bot Preference Sync while allowing accountable mixed-use crawlers to remain available for search, whereas the broader Block setting can stop mixed-use crawlers such as Googlebot, Bingbot and Applebot entirely. The operational lesson is to govern Search, Training and Agent traffic separately instead of treating every AI-related crawler as one category.
explanation: What changed: Cloudflare added a Disallow AI Training option to its more granular Search, Training and Agent crawler controls. Cloudflare says Bot Preference Sync publishes the applicable no-training preference in robots.txt, accountable mixed-use crawlers remain allowed for search, and other training crawlers are blocked. The same announcement warns that the broader Block and Block on pages with ads settings now apply to mixed-use crawlers too, so those choices can affect search discovery as well as training.

Why it matters: search visibility and AI-training permission are related but not identical business decisions. A blanket bot rule can unintentionally remove a site from useful discovery surfaces if the same crawler supports both search and another use. For a company investing in SEO, GEO, AEO and AI visibility, the safer operating model is to decide explicitly which traffic is allowed for Search, which is allowed for Training, and which Agent behavior is acceptable, then verify the actual crawl result instead of assuming every 'AI bot' label means the same thing.

What to do: audit the current Cloudflare AI Crawl Control and Bot Preference Sync settings before changing robots behavior. If the goal is to remain searchable while refusing training, evaluate Disallow AI Training rather than a blanket Block. After any change, verify robots.txt, Google and Bing crawlability, Search Console or Bing Webmaster evidence, and server or Cloudflare crawl logs. Keep Agent policy separate because Cloudflare says the Internet does not yet have a well-established directive for expressing a universal disallow preference to agents.

Result: site owners can apply a more precise governance policy without intentionally sacrificing search crawlability. This is not a ranking guarantee and it does not mean every crawler will behave identically; it creates a clearer technical policy that can be measured and audited. The website remains the canonical source, while search and AI systems receive the permissions the owner actually intends.

Historical context: Hermes marketing and search operating material has repeatedly treated discoverability, owned-site control and platform distribution as connected work. The earlier tradeoff was often framed too coarsely as allow or block. The September 2026 Cloudflare controls make that operating decision more granular. Historical private metrics, client details and old platform claims are not reused here; the current capability and limits come from Cloudflare's dated public documentation.
takeaways: Cloudflare announced Disallow AI Training on September 15, 2026 for separating training preferences from search access
Cloudflare says broader Block settings can now affect mixed-use crawlers such as Googlebot, Bingbot and Applebot, including search
Audit Search, Training and Agent controls separately instead of applying one blanket AI-bot rule
After any crawler-policy change, verify robots.txt and real search crawl evidence; do not treat the setting as a rankings guarantee

faq.question: Does Disallow AI Training block Googlebot or Bingbot from search?
faq.answer: Cloudflare says accountable mixed-use crawlers can remain allowed for search under Disallow AI Training while a no-training preference is published. A broader Block setting can stop mixed-use crawlers entirely, including their search use.

faq.question: Does this guarantee that a site will rank better in Google or Bing?
faq.answer: No. The setting governs crawler access and training preferences; it does not guarantee rankings, impressions, Discover exposure or traffic.

faq.question: How does Cloudflare express the no-training preference?
faq.answer: Cloudflare says Bot Preference Sync publishes the applicable preference in robots.txt and pairs that stated preference with its crawler controls.

faq.question: Should Agent traffic be treated the same as Training traffic?
faq.answer: Not automatically. Cloudflare separates Search, Training and Agent controls and says there is not yet a well-established Internet-wide directive for expressing the same Disallow preference to agents.

title: Dry Van Spot Rates: $2.17/Mile Carrier Analysis | Hermes
description: DAT reported dry-van spot linehaul averaging $2.17 per mile for the week ending September 18, 2026, down slightly week over week but still materially above the year-earlier and seasonal benchmarks.
h1: Dry van spot linehaul eased to $2.17 per mile. What should carriers do now?
conciseAnswer: DAT reported U.S. dry-van spot linehaul averaging $2.17 per mile for the week ending September 18, 2026, excluding fuel. That was down $0.03, or 1.2%, week over week, while remaining $0.53, or 32.8%, above a year earlier and $0.36 above DAT's nine-year seasonal average. The useful decision is still lane-specific: compare loaded miles, deadhead, fuel, tolls, timing, equipment fit, payment terms and the likely next move rather than treating a national average as a universal booking target.
explanation: What changed: DAT reported dry-van spot linehaul paid to carriers averaging $2.17 per mile for the week ending September 18, 2026, excluding fuel. The national average fell $0.03 per mile, or 1.2%, from the prior week. At the same time, it remained $0.53 per mile, or 32.8%, above the year-earlier level and $0.36 per mile above DAT's nine-year seasonal average of $1.82. That combination matters because a soft week-over-week move can coexist with a market that is still comparatively firm over a longer horizon.

Why it matters: a single national number is not a lane quote. DAT's regional data for the same week ranged from $2.66 per mile in the Great Lakes and $2.64 in the Ohio River region to $1.42 in Florida–South Georgia. A carrier can therefore see a strong national or origin-region headline while still accepting a movement that produces weak round-trip economics because of destination demand, deadhead, appointment timing or the quality of the next reload.

Historical Hermes operating material repeatedly treated route planning, deadhead reduction, broker negotiation and the next reload as one decision chain. The then-versus-now lesson is not that an old internal rate or earnings target should be reused. It is that the same operating discipline becomes more valuable when the market is moving in different directions across time horizons and regions: verify the lane, understand where the truck lands, and price the full movement rather than one loaded segment.

What to do: use DAT's current market average as an external reference point, then calculate the actual movement. Separate loaded miles from deadhead to pickup and likely repositioning after delivery. Add current fuel and toll assumptions, time requirements, equipment constraints and payment terms. Compare realistic reload options in the destination market before negotiating. A counteroffer is more defensible when it is tied to the truck's real operating picture instead of a national headline alone.

Result: the carrier gets a repeatable decision process instead of a reactive rate rule. The September 21 DAT update says the national dry-van linehaul average eased slightly after a strong year-over-year rise; it does not say every lane is weakening or that every load should target $2.17. The practical outcome is to refresh lane assumptions more often, keep deadhead visible in the calculation, and use current regional context to decide where the national average is useful and where it is misleading.
takeaways: $2.17 per mile was DAT's national dry-van spot linehaul average for the week ending September 18; fuel was excluded
The average fell 1.2% week over week but remained 32.8% above the year-earlier level and 19.7% above the nine-year seasonal average
Regional averages varied materially, including $2.66 in the Great Lakes versus $1.42 in Florida–South Georgia
Use the market report to refresh lane assumptions, then calculate the full movement with deadhead, costs, timing and reload options

faq.answer: No. DAT's national average is market context, not a universal floor. A load decision depends on the specific lane, deadhead, fuel, tolls, equipment, timing, payment terms, operating costs and the likely next movement.

faq.answer: No. DAT states that the cited dry-van spot linehaul rates exclude fuel costs and surcharges unless otherwise noted.

faq.question: Why does regional data matter if the national rate is current?
faq.answer: Because the week ending September 18 showed large regional differences. A national average can describe the broad market while still being a poor proxy for a specific origin, destination or round-trip opportunity.

title: FMCSA Fuel HOS Waiver: What Carriers Need to Know | Hermes
description: FMCSA issued a temporary hours-of-service waiver for interstate carriers and drivers transporting gasoline and diesel fuel from September 16 through December 16, 2026. Hermes explains the scope, safety conditions, and dispatch implications without treating it as a general trucking HOS exemption.
h1: FMCSA changed hours-of-service flexibility for fuel hauling. Who is actually covered?
conciseAnswer: FMCSA issued a temporary waiver from 49 CFR 395.3 for interstate motor carriers and drivers transporting gasoline and diesel fuel. It runs from September 16 through December 16, 2026, and is narrow: it does not create a general HOS exemption for freight. Covered drivers may not drive more than 16 hours in any 24-hour period and must follow the waiver's rest, eligibility, documentation, and safety conditions.
explanation: What changed: On September 16, 2026, FMCSA granted a temporary waiver from the hours-of-service limitations in 49 CFR 395.3 for interstate motor carriers and drivers transporting gasoline and diesel fuel. The waiver is effective through December 16, 2026. It is tied to fuel transportation and does not remove other Federal Motor Carrier Safety Regulations or hazardous-material requirements.

Why it matters: Dispatchers and carriers can create a compliance problem if they treat a narrow waiver as permission to extend every driver's day. FMCSA's conditions include a 16-hour maximum driving limit in any 24-hour period, minimum rest requirements, valid CDL and required endorsements, possession of a copy of the waiver, safety-rating eligibility, immediate rest when requested, transition rules back to normal operations, and crash-reporting duties.

What to do: Before a dispatcher changes a schedule, first verify that the movement is actually gasoline or diesel fuel transportation covered by the waiver and that the carrier and driver meet the eligibility conditions. Keep the waiver available to the driver, preserve the required rest window, track the transition back to normal HOS operations, and continue following every regulation that FMCSA did not waive.

Result: The useful operational outcome is not 'more driving hours' in the abstract. It is a clearly documented decision tree: covered fuel movement, eligible carrier and driver, waiver conditions met, safe schedule built, and normal HOS rules restored correctly after waiver operations. That reduces the risk of applying a temporary exception to the wrong load or driver.

Historical context: Hermes operating archives have long treated routing, scheduling and driver communication as connected dispatch decisions. The 2026 waiver changes the compliance envelope for a narrow fuel-hauling segment, but it does not change the underlying discipline: verify the rule that applies before changing the plan. No historical rates, earnings, private contacts, or old compliance claims are reused as current facts.
takeaways: The waiver applies to interstate transportation of gasoline and diesel fuel, not freight generally
It is effective September 16 through December 16, 2026
Covered drivers may not drive more than 16 hours in any 24-hour period and must meet the waiver's rest and eligibility conditions
Dispatch should verify scope and conditions before changing a driver's schedule

faq.question: Does the waiver let every truck driver work a 16-hour driving day?
faq.answer: No. The waiver is limited to qualifying interstate operations transporting gasoline and diesel fuel, and covered carriers and drivers must comply with its terms and conditions.

faq.question: When does the FMCSA waiver expire?
faq.answer: FMCSA states that it expires at 11:59 p.m. on December 16, 2026.

faq.question: What rest is required under the waiver?
faq.answer: FMCSA requires at least 6 consecutive hours in the sleeper berth in each 24-hour period, or at least 8 consecutive hours off duty if there is no sleeper berth. Additional 10-hour rest requirements apply in specified circumstances, including when a driver requests immediate rest and when transitioning back to normal operations after reaching the stated threshold.

faq.question: Does the waiver replace CDL, hazmat, insurance, drug-testing or other safety rules?
faq.answer: No. FMCSA expressly states that requirements not specifically waived remain in force, including CDL, controlled-substance and alcohol testing, financial responsibility, hazardous-material rules, vehicle size and weight rules, and other applicable Federal and State requirements.

title: Meta One Business Tools: What Changes for Organic Social | Hermes
description: Meta introduced Meta One with new professional tools for creators and businesses, including enhanced profiles, stronger follow conversion features and, on higher plans, advanced publishing and analytics capabilities. Hermes explains what the September 2026 rollout changes for organic social operations.
h1: Meta One adds professional publishing and conversion tools. What should organic social teams change?
conciseAnswer: Meta announced Meta One on September 15, 2026, with plans for creators and businesses rolling out globally. Meta says the offering includes professional presence and conversion features such as enhanced profiles, a more prominent follow button on Reels and automatic follow invitations for people who interact with content; higher business tiers add capabilities such as Story scheduling, links in organic posts and Reels, exportable analytics, deeper audience insights and team access. Availability varies by region, app and account.
explanation: What changed: Meta introduced Meta One as a subscription layer across its apps with plans for individuals, creators and businesses. For business and creator accounts, Meta describes tools aimed at building presence and turning attention into action: enhanced profile information, a prominent follow button on Reels, automatic follow invitations for people who engage, and expanded access to Meta Business Agent. Meta also lists advanced publishing, analytics and team-access capabilities in higher business tiers.

Why it matters: Organic social work is increasingly becoming an operating system, not just a posting calendar. Scheduling, profile conversion, analytics export, audience analysis and controlled team access can reduce operational friction, but none of those features create demand by themselves. The underlying job remains to earn relevant attention, understand which content brings qualified audiences, and connect that attention to a measurable business action.

What to do: Do not buy a subscription just because a feature exists. First identify the bottleneck: publishing consistency, profile conversion, measurement, team access or customer response. Then check which Meta One features are actually available to the account and region, compare them with the current workflow, and test only the feature that can remove a measurable bottleneck. Keep content, audience and conversion metrics separate so a convenience feature is not mistaken for marketing performance.

Result: A disciplined team can use the new tools to shorten production and measurement loops while keeping strategy independent of the platform subscription. The target outcome is faster publishing, cleaner account access, better measurement and clearer conversion paths—not simply more posts or a paid badge.

Historical context: Hermes marketing archives previously emphasized consistent organic publishing, audience interaction and content-native optimization as recurring operating work. Meta One moves more of the execution layer—publishing controls, profile conversion and analytics—inside Meta's paid toolset. The method still starts with useful content and audience fit; the platform is changing how teams can execute and measure it. Historical pricing, case metrics and private client figures are not reused here.
takeaways: Meta One creator and business plans are rolling out globally, with availability varying by region, app and account
Meta says business tools include enhanced profiles, stronger follow conversion and expanded Meta Business Agent access
Higher tiers can include Story scheduling, links in organic posts and Reels, exportable analytics, deeper audience insights and team access

faq.question: Does Meta One replace organic social strategy?
faq.answer: No. Meta One adds tools and higher usage limits. Content relevance, audience fit, creative quality, measurement and conversion design still determine whether social activity creates business value.

faq.question: Can every business account use every Meta One feature immediately?
faq.answer: No. Meta says plans and features are rolling out and that availability can vary by region, app and account. Teams should verify what is offered inside the specific account before changing a workflow.

faq.question: What is most useful for an organic social team?
faq.answer: That depends on the bottleneck. Publishing teams may value scheduling and team access; growth teams may value follow-conversion tools; analysts may value exportable analytics and deeper audience insights. The right test is the one tied to a measurable workflow or conversion problem.

faq.question: Should a team publish more just because scheduling becomes easier?
faq.answer: Not automatically. Lower publishing friction is useful only if the additional content remains relevant, differentiated and measurable. A stronger cadence without audience value can create more activity without better business outcomes.

title: Google Search Profile Badge: Connect Website and Social | Hermes Insights
description: Google documented a Search profile badge that lets eligible site owners point visitors to a Search profile combining content from their website and linked social platforms.
h1: Google can now connect a Search profile with your website and social content. What should brands do?
conciseAnswer: Google Search Central added documentation on September 16, 2026 for site owners, publishers and creators who have a Search profile. Google says a Search profile brings together content from a website and linked social platforms, and that when readers follow the profile, linked content can be more likely to appear for that audience in Google Discover. A badge can point website visitors to the claimed profile, but it is not a ranking guarantee.
explanation: What changed: Google published a guide for website owners, publishers and creators with a Search profile to add an official Search profile badge to their site. Google describes the Search profile as a destination that can bring together content from a website and linked platforms including Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, X and Facebook. The badge should be added only after the Search profile has been claimed and should follow Google's branding and accessibility guidance.

Why it matters: social content and the owned website no longer need to be treated as completely separate discovery surfaces. Google says that when people follow a Search profile, content linked on that profile can be more likely to appear for that audience in Discover. That creates a practical identity-and-distribution connection, but it does not mean adding the badge automatically improves rankings, impressions or leads.

What to do: first verify whether the brand has an eligible Search profile and claim it. Then audit the website and linked social identities for consistent naming, ownership and current URLs. If the profile is claimed, add the official badge or text link in a place where users can understand what it does. Measure Search/Discover visibility and downstream visits separately from social engagement so the team can tell whether the connection changes discovery behavior.

Result: the website remains the canonical owned destination while the Search profile can act as a Google-facing bridge to verified social content. Historical Hermes marketing work already emphasized consistent original publishing and connecting social activity to an owned business presence; the 2026 Search profile feature adds a new distribution layer to that pattern without validating any old growth guarantee, pricing claim or private client metric.

faq.question: Does adding the Search profile badge improve Google rankings?
faq.answer: Google's documentation does not promise a ranking increase. The badge helps users find a claimed Search profile, and Google says following that profile can make linked content more likely to appear for that audience in Discover.

faq.question: Which social platforms can appear on a Search profile?
faq.answer: Google's guide gives Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, X and Facebook as examples of content that can be linked on a Search profile, along with the website.

faq.question: Can every website add the badge immediately?
faq.answer: The guide is for website owners, publishers or creators with a Search profile. Google instructs users to claim the Search profile first, then use the profile URL and official badge assets.
